lane: tectonic-geomorphology: channel steepness and knickpoints (Kirby & Whipple 2012; Perron & Royden 2013; Gailleton et al. 2019)
hypothesis: Bedrock-channel steepness and knickpoints record spatial gradients in rock uplift, so a base-level step left by an active fault is still present in the channel profile after the surface scarp has degraded and buried. Knickpoint crossings that align across several independent drainages along a common strike therefore locate faults - including ones the USGS/INGENIOUS catalogue omits.
mechanism: Chi transform puts channels on a comparable footing; in chi-space the profile slope is the normalised steepness ksn = (U/K)^(1/n). A fault crossing a channel produces a break in the chi-profile; the crossing is projected along the local channel NORMAL and reinforced where independent drainages share a strike, which is the operational form of 'align across several independent drainages'.
named_non_fault_process_that_could_mimic: Two, both named in the brief and both measured here. (1) Internal-drainage / playa base levels: a playa sets base level by evaporation, so it manufactures base-level steps with no tectonic cause. Measured: the priority-flood fill raises 899,623 cells (17.4 % of the valid grid) - the Great Basin's closed basins. (2) Lithologic (erodibility) contrast: ksn ~ (U/K)^(1/n), so a rock-type change with no uplift change mimics a fault. Not masked in this run; listed as hypothesis 5.
